source.title: Subliminal Learning: LLMs Transmit Behavioral Traits via Hidden Signals in Data

record.file_problem: The supplied text is a complete-looking Alignment Forum cross-post and comments, not the full linked paper; no garbling or cutoff is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The post reports the original intervention: fine-tuning students on filtered, teacher-generated outputs and evaluating whether they acquire the teacher's traits.
record.gate_note: The post mostly summarizes results qualitatively and refers readers to the paper for details. It gives no plotted values from Figures 2–4. Claims from commenters about their own replications are not treated as study results.
record.test_reason: This is the original authors' cross-post of the source paper (arXiv:2507.14805). It reports that paper's own experiments: filtered teacher outputs, same-base students, and trait evaluation. Because it is the original source, no verdict labels are given.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. Filtered, semantically unrelated model-generated data transmits traits, including misalignment, when teacher and student share a base model. The signal lies in model-specific statistical patterns, so filtering may be insufficient.
record.recipe_differences: The post describes the original setup: prompt or fine-tune a teacher to exhibit a trait, generate narrow-domain data, filter trait references, fine-tune the same initial model, and evaluate for the trait.
record.method_sensitivity: The post reports that transmission fails across different base models, while GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o show cross-model transmission that may reflect a shared training checkpoint.

fits_no_version.finding: An MNIST student learns digit classification despite training with no class logits and no digit inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subliminal transmission occurs in small non-LLM networks that share an initialisation.

record.problems: The post is a summary rather than the full paper and supplies few numerical results; referenced figures have no plotted values in the provided text. The cross-model significance description applies only to Figure 4 and reports N ≥ 5 runs per setting.
record.rows_left_out: No further study results omitted. Results reported only by commenters as their own replications were excluded.

untested.parts: No prompt-only (no fine-tuning) insertion of linked tokens is reported.
No full fine-tuning vs LoRA comparison, no LoRA-rank comparison, and no explicit test of evaluation prompts unlike the training prompts.
No empirical identification of the carrier (token entanglement, divergence tokens, steering direction); only the gradient theorem and the MNIST demonstration.

missing.what: Replication with fine-tuned (rather than system-prompted) animal teachers, said to work (paper Fig. 14).
missing.locator: Comments, cloud reply on fine-tuned animal teachers

missing.what: Co-author reports failed transmission of 'wealth seeking behavior' and collateral transfer (owl numbers raise preference for other birds).
Co-author reports eliciting the trait more easily with evaluation prompts in-distribution with training (number prefix used for Qwen2.5 7B).
In-context learning on the teacher data fails to detect or transmit traits.

record.verdict_notes: This post is an author summary of the original source paper, so no verdicts are given under the rules. Rows are mostly qualitative with no figure values. The cross-base results (r7–r9) bear on B, not A. Commenter replications by non-authors (e.g. faul_sname's owl logprobs) are not study results.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not give per-animal, per-model, or per-dataset numerical results.
It does not report a systematic comparison across all combinations of model families or a precise definition of how similar base models must be.
The post gives no numerical misalignment rates or detailed breakdown by teacher, student, or evaluation prompt.
The post presents a gradient-descent theorem and evidence consistent with model-specific signals, but does not identify the empirical signal or establish a specific token-level mechanism.
Evaluation across many prompts is asserted, but full fine-tuning comparisons, LoRA-rank comparisons, and prompt-set details are not stated.
No student prompt-only experiment without fine-tuning is reported.

relation.reason: Its own results (shown in figures and stated in words) bear on A, B and C, and it describes the theorem and MNIST result for D.

tranche.reason: This is the original authors' cross-post. It reports the original's own experiments (teacher with a trait, filtered narrow-domain data, same-base student, trait evaluation). As an original source it is a baseline, so no verdicts apply.

source_check.notes: The post states no result numbers in its text; results are in figures only, and r8 rests on an author comment. Author comments also report that 'wealth seeking behavior' failed to transmit, and that the Qwen2.5-7B evaluation needed an in-distribution 'Here are 3 numbers' prefix. Both are relevant to the scope of A and E but are not recorded as rows.

statements.correction: The post body says the nano-teacher data transmit to a nano student 'but not to a student based on Qwen2.5'. The post also reports cross-model transmission between GPT-4.1 and GPT-4o, attributed to a likely shared checkpoint (r9). An author comment reports no transfer among GPT-4.1, 4.1 mini and 4.1 nano, which share a tokenizer (r8). The post states no numbers.
statements.problem: The only sentence about this study (a nano teacher does not reliably transmit to a Qwen2.5 student, r7) matches the post. All numbers belong to the preprint or Nature version. r8 and r9 are cited but not described.

statements.correction: Post: a teacher fine-tuned on insecure code transmits misalignment through filtered, aligned, correct CoT traces (Figure 3), and also through numbers with numbers like '666' removed. Misalignment rates appear only in the left panel of Figure 3; the right panel gives examples. The text states no rate. There is no misalignment result with code as the carrier.
statements.problem: It says this post's r6 shows misalignment through code. In the post, 'insecure code' is how the teacher was made misaligned; the data that carry the trait are CoT and numbers, not code. The conclusion still stands: no code-carrier misalignment result is reported.
